1: The best group of bats in the league sits in Myrtle Beach, which slides a spot to No. 5 because the pitching side is so thin. Erik Fisher (No. 1), the first overall pick in the 2032 Draft, is the top prospect in the game, with elite power, gap power and discipline, a plus hit tool and plus outfield defense, and he hit .304/.419/.622 with 21 homers this season, now at Double-A. Josh Dean (No. 27) has an elite hit tool but below-average power, Ben Sloan (No. 98) is a 19-year-old with elite hit and plate discipline at A-, and Lear Eichhorn (No. 85) has elite discipline. Curt Barber (No. 119), with elite stuff and a plus slider, is the lone arm among eight top-200 names, which explains why the pitching rank is 23rd and balance grades well below average.
2: Pitching drives Chicago's two-spot climb to No. 11: six of its eight top-200 prospects are arms, and the pitching group ranks third in the league. Roberto Garcia (No. 20) is an 18-year-old at Rookie ball with plus stuff, movement and stamina and an elite fastball and curve, and he posted a 2.29 ERA over 63 innings. Isaiah Cunning (No. 23), the 16th overall pick in the 2032 Draft, has plus movement at Double-A, and Jared Milligan (No. 116) combines a plus fastball, elite curve and plus splitter with a 1.66 ERA in 59 2/3 innings. The lineup is the weak side, ranking 28th, though Kris Cavanaugh (No. 34), the 23rd overall pick in 2032, has elite gap power and hit .448/.572/.828 with 19 homers in 232 at-bats. Four Top 100 prospects round it out.
3: Philadelphia takes the steepest fall in the rankings, down eight spots since mid-July to No. 17, tied with New Orleans, and what remains is a system with one headliner and little behind him. Edwin Martinez (No. 4) is the standout, a Triple-A starter with elite control and plus movement and stamina, but a 4.60 ERA with 4.8 strikeouts per nine suggests his results lag the tools. John Shannon (No. 44), a catcher at Triple-A, hit .254/.330/.385 this season, and Cesar Cabrera (No. 146), a second-round pick in the 2032 Draft, offers a plus hit tool, elite gap power and plus speed at Rookie ball. With only three top-200 names, readiness ranked 26th and a below-average depth grade, the Eagles need a stronger draft and development run to recover.
4: Two pitchers are all Spokane has in the top 200, yet the system rises four spots to No. 23. Jonathan Montano (No. 22), the lone Top 100 name, is a 22-year-old Triple-A starter with plus movement, elite stamina and a plus fastball, slider and sinker, and he logged 154 innings with a 4.32 ERA. Aaron Myers (No. 148), the 14th overall pick in the 2032 Draft, has plus control and a plus fastball at A- but is only 18 and still working through a 3.91 ERA in 50 2/3 innings. There are no hitters in the top 200, and a below-average blue-chip grade and a batting rank of 26th make that the plainest gap; the Sasquatches need bats and more arms behind Montano to move up again.
5: Vancouver gives back one spot since mid-July, slipping to No. 4, yet it still carries more top-200 prospects than any other system, 12 in all, eight of them in the Top 100. Elite blue-chip talent and elite depth anchor the group, which is built around outfielders: Jeremy Austin (No. 26) pairs elite gap power with plus power, discipline and speed, and Micah Patterson (No. 29) adds a plus hit tool and plus speed, both at A-. Kyle Gregson (No. 59), an A- infielder with a plus hit tool, hit .373 with 15 homers in 158 at-bats. On the mound, Jarrod Bensel (No. 15) has reached the big leagues with elite stamina and a plus changeup and sinker, and Jim White (No. 52), a second-round pick in the 2032 Draft, is a plus defensive catcher at Double-A.
6: Toronto holds at No. 8, with a sixth-ranked pitching group carrying more weight than the lineup. Brent Michalski (No. 14) is a Triple-A starter with elite control and plus movement, though his stuff grades below average and he put up a 4.70 ERA with only 5.3 strikeouts per nine. Ron Turner (No. 35) is the more intriguing arm: a 19-year-old at Double-A with an elite fastball, plus slider, plus movement and plus stamina who worked 128 1/3 innings with a 3.79 ERA. Mike Larson (No. 17) has an elite hit tool and elite gap power, yet below-average power and plate discipline held his season line to .240/.311/.344. Pat Heick (No. 199), the 19th overall pick in the 2032 Draft, adds elite power at Rookie ball. Three Top 100 prospects and a plus balance grade offset average depth.
7: With no arms among its five top-200 prospects, Virginia holds at No. 31 and owns the league's weakest pitching and readiness marks. Jameson Towne (No. 53), a fourth-round pick in the 2032 Draft, is the lone Top 100 name, a Triple-A center fielder with elite gap power, plus speed and plus defense who hit .322/.376/.537 this season. Travis McLaughlin (No. 156), a 19-year-old at A, has plus hit, gap power and speed and hit .318/.399/.543, and Travis Tucker (No. 144) offers elite power and plus discipline at A+ despite a .221 average. Jalen Jones (No. 194) is a plus-glove infielder at Double-A. Blue-chip, depth and balance grades all come in well below average, which is the Rebels' problem in a sentence: very little is close, and nothing is on the mound.
8: Baltimore slips one spot to No. 7 but owns the second-best readiness mark in the league. Rick D'Amore (No. 21), a Double-A infielder, combines plus power with elite gap power and discipline and hit .306/.428/.534 with 22 homers this season, while Danny Cox (No. 32) has already reached the big leagues with a plus hit tool and plus speed. David Manley (No. 82), a 25-year-old outfielder, hit .346/.411/.608, and Chris Davis (No. 89) added a .329/.415/.532 line with 18 homers. Relievers Jayden Todd (No. 124), who has a plus slider, and Manny Diaz (No. 139), with a 1.35 ERA, give the group bullpen depth. Plus blue-chip talent and plus depth carry the ranking, but a below-average balance grade shows how tilted toward hitters it is.
9: Eight of New Orleans' nine top-200 prospects are hitters, a lopsided mix that goes with an eight-spot fall to No. 18, tied with Philadelphia for the steepest drop; the batting rank is fourth, the pitching rank 27th. Alejandro Vargas (No. 5) has elite gap power and speed with plus hit, power and discipline and has reached the majors, though he hit just .217/.321/.306 this season, and Matt Kulp (No. 43), who also reached the big leagues, hit .221. Dave McCloy (No. 62) hit .301/.371/.500 with 17 homers at Triple-A, while 2032 draftees Michael Herr (No. 121) and Adam Elliott (No. 166) both reached A+, Herr with a .305/.377/.545 line and Elliott with elite plate discipline. A well-below-average balance grade captures the problem: one pitcher among nine names.
10: Milwaukee moves up two spots to No. 19 with a compact system: four top-200 names, three of them in the Top 100, and an eighth-ranked readiness mark that reflects how many sit at Triple-A. Manuel Ruiz (No. 28) leads with an elite hit tool, plus gap power and plus speed at Double-A, and he hit .282/.367/.399 this season. Larry Leppert Jr. (No. 42), the lone arm, has plus movement, control and stamina and a plus fastball and changeup, and he turned in a 3.52 ERA over 150 2/3 innings with only 4.7 strikeouts per nine. Jason Klamm (No. 61) and Vince Gilroy (No. 117), both Triple-A bats with plus speed, give the group near-term options. Average blue-chip, depth and balance grades sum it up: nothing is broken, but there is not much top-end talent either.
11: Upside has yet to show up in the results for Denver, which falls three spots to No. 26. Gustavo Perez (No. 36), a 20-year-old outfielder at A-, has plus power, elite gap power, elite discipline and plus speed but hit just .224/.336/.345 in 116 at-bats this season. Alex Suazo (No. 55) has pitched well, a 22-year-old at A+ with plus movement and control, elite stamina and a 2.72 ERA over 109 innings despite below-average stuff. Dylan McCreedy (No. 126) is a plus defensive catcher who hit 17 homers, and Odilon Keating (No. 132), a 17-year-old at the international complex, has elite plate discipline. Two Top 100 prospects, a below-average depth grade and a readiness rank of 24th suggest the payoff is still well down the road.
12: Oahu holds the No. 1 spot it occupied in mid-July, and the Paddlers do it with arms: their pitching group ranks first in the league. Casey Emerson (No. 7) has plus stuff and movement along with a plus slider, changeup, cutter and sinker, and he posted a 3.54 ERA over 109 1/3 innings. Oliver Zimmer (No. 12), the second overall pick in the 2032 Draft, owns a 2.85 ERA, and Gary Walters (No. 18) fans 11.3 per nine on an elite fastball and cutter even though his control grades below average. Carlos Navarro (No. 9), a 20-year-old center fielder, has elite hit, gap power and speed but below-average over-the-fence power. Eight Top 100 prospects and elite blue-chip and balance grades define the system, though readiness ranks only 13th.
13: Las Vegas holds at No. 14 with a system that is deeper than it is dazzling: plus depth, a fifth-ranked readiness mark and an average balance grade, but below-average blue-chip talent and only two Top 100 prospects. Bryan Kiestler (No. 76), the ninth overall pick in the 2032 Draft, is the best of them, a center fielder with plus discipline and a plus glove who hit .313/.415/.538 with 18 homers this season and now sits at A+. Ken Grossman (No. 73), the lone pitcher in the group, has plus control and stamina and a 3.47 ERA at Double-A. Steve Mendoza (No. 104), a plus defensive catcher with a plus hit tool, and Eric Spangenberg (No. 141), whose speed grades elite, round out a group that is close to the majors but light on impact.
14: Galveston ties Montreal for the largest climb, up six spots to No. 16, even though the base is thin: only three prospects reach the top 200 and just one reaches the Top 100. Chris Hein (No. 19), the 20th overall pick in the 2032 Draft, carries the system, a Double-A infielder with plus hit, power and plate discipline who hit .268/.343/.408 with eight homers this season. Matthew Tenner (No. 108) has already reached the big leagues with plus control and elite stamina, and Nate Krogh (No. 155), a second-round pick in 2032, pairs elite movement with plus control and stamina out of the bullpen even though his stuff grades well below average. A ninth-place readiness mark helps, but below-average blue-chip talent and an average depth grade show a system that needs more arrivals before it can climb further.
15: Oklahoma City dips one spot to No. 12, and the story is catchers and readiness. The Outlaws have the third-best readiness mark in the league and three catchers among its seven highest-ranked prospects: Lee Hughes (No. 64), a second-round pick in the 2032 Draft with a plus catch-and-throw grade who hit .345/.455/.473 this season, Tom Guier (No. 68), a Triple-A bat with 15 homers, and Ken Landreth (No. 118), another plus defender behind the plate. Mark Barnes (No. 69), the 28th overall pick in 2032, offers plus power, elite gap power and plus discipline at A+. The pitching is workmanlike, led by Felix Rosario (No. 114), whose elite stamina and plus slider and changeup produced a 4.05 ERA. Three Top 100 prospects and average blue-chip talent, lifted by plus depth, make this a system built on volume rather than stars.
16: Tampa Bay climbs two spots to No. 24 on the back of a respectable lineup, with batting ranked 14th against a pitching rank of 26th and readiness ranked 30th. Robby Clem (No. 30), a 25-year-old at Triple-A with plus hit, power, gap power and discipline, is the top bat, though he hit just .266/.328/.384 this season. Doug Fleury (No. 92) hit 20 homers with plus power, discipline and speed but a below-average hit tool, and Bryan Clausen (No. 138), a third-round pick in the 2032 Draft, has plus power and gap power at Rookie ball. The pitching side is a single name, Ryan Affrunti (No. 79), who has plus movement and control and elite stamina but below-average stuff and a 5.39 ERA. With three Top 100 prospects but very little close to the majors, the Cannons are building for later.
17: Cincinnati has no pitchers among its four top-200 prospects, and the system slips a spot to No. 29; the pitching rank is 30th. Bobby Avila (No. 38), a 17-year-old outfielder at Rookie ball, is the headliner with plus power and gap power, elite discipline and a .258/.371/.403 line this season. Mauricio Dominguez (No. 41) is a plus defensive catcher at Triple-A, Josh Boucher (No. 83) has elite power and plus speed and defense but a below-average hit tool, and Matt Bellefeuille (No. 163) has reached the big leagues after hitting .332/.401/.575 this season. Three Top 100 prospects keep the floor from collapsing, but well-below-average depth and balance grades show how much the Regents need arms to rebuild the pipeline.
18: San Juan rises two spots to No. 10 behind a lineup that is better than its balance grade suggests. Adam Rall (No. 6), a Triple-A infielder with a plus hit tool, plus power, elite gap power and plus discipline, hit .261/.333/.467 with 20 homers this season. Jeff Blanchard (No. 129) hit .338/.408/.542 on an elite hit tool, and Joel Babb (No. 47), the 13th overall pick in the 2032 Draft, brings elite plate discipline and plus power to Rookie ball, though he hit just .204 in 152 at-bats. The arms are thinner: Matt Giglio (No. 93), a 19-year-old reliever, has an elite fastball and a 2.87 ERA but control that grades below average, and Daniel Shuping (No. 142) has elite stamina but a fragile durability grade. Four Top 100 prospects and plus blue-chip talent anchor a bat-first system.
19: Southland climbs one spot to No. 6 on elite depth: ten top-200 prospects, eight of them hitters, even though only three reach the Top 100. Christian Lombera (No. 10), a Triple-A infielder, is the headliner with elite power, a plus hit tool and plus gap power and discipline, and he hit .271/.357/.397 with 10 homers this season. Geoff Fawcett (No. 75) is a 19-year-old with elite gap power and discipline at A, and Mario Canton (No. 115) hit .300/.358/.492 with 16 homers as a center fielder with plus speed and defense. The arm side is thin: Chris Enriquez (No. 88) has plus movement and a plus changeup but below-average stuff and a 4.64 ERA. Readiness ranks 27th, so little of this group is close.
20: Somerville moves up two spots since mid-July to No. 3 and owns the best readiness mark in the league, with elite depth behind it. This is a bat-first group, with seven of its 10 top-200 names on the hitting side, led by Kevin Miller (No. 8), a 22-year-old outfielder with plus hit, power, discipline and speed and elite gap power who hit .310/.386/.535 with 23 homers this season. Willie Schultz (No. 51) hit .335/.422/.523, and Eric Aasen (No. 37), a plus defensive catcher, has already reached the big leagues. The arm to watch is Sebastian Croslin (No. 60): elite stuff, stamina, fastball and curve and a 1.86 ERA with 12.4 strikeouts per nine, but control that grades well below average. Seven Top 100 prospects show a system that leans heavily on its lineup.
21: Memphis climbs three spots to No. 13, powered by two infielders who both rank inside the league's top 20. Mike Jenkins (No. 13) has already reached the big leagues and hit .329/.399/.500 this season with an elite hit tool, elite gap power and plus discipline, even though his over-the-fence power grades well below average. Chris Faulk (No. 16) has plus hit and discipline, elite gap power and elite speed at A+, and he hit .333/.424/.532. Tom Morrison (No. 65) offers elite gap power and a plus glove at A, and Pedro Miranda (No. 66) has plus stuff, stamina and a plus fastball and cutter at Double-A. Four Top 100 names and plus blue-chip talent are encouraging, but readiness ranks 28th, so most of this group remains a step or more away.
22: One elite arm now carries Boston, which drops four spots to No. 21. Josh Owens (No. 2), the second-best prospect in the game, has plus stuff, movement and control, elite stamina and an elite curve and splitter at Triple-A, and he posted a 3.01 ERA over 86 2/3 innings. Behind him are Jesse Simson (No. 94) and Eric Behnke (No. 182), two hitters with elite gap power and plus speed, and reliever Bill Barraza (No. 171), who pairs an elite fastball with a 2.75 ERA. The lineup is the weak spot, ranking 29th, and a below-average depth grade shows how little there is beyond the top. An elite balance grade is a small positive for a group split evenly between two hitters and two pitchers.
23: Big Horn jumps four spots to No. 15, helped by a sixth-ranked readiness mark and the league's tenth-best pitching group. The arms are the clearest strength: Jeremy Johnston (No. 74) has plus movement and control and posted a 3.42 ERA with just 1.9 walks per nine, Justin Barth (No. 111) pairs plus control with a plus fastball and sinker and has already reached the big leagues, and Steve Fox (No. 147) brings an elite fastball and curve out of the bullpen despite a 4.76 ERA. Geoff Danser (No. 70), a 20-year-old center fielder with elite gap power and a plus glove, leads the bats, and Sean Miles (No. 39), a fourth-round pick in the 2032 Draft, hit .295/.368/.450. Three Top 100 prospects and average blue-chip and depth grades keep it mid-pack, with a plus balance grade.
24: Fort Collins stays at No. 2, and its argument for the top spot is its arms, which rank second in the league, backed by elite grades in blue-chip talent, depth and balance. R.J. Blum (No. 3) is the headliner, a Triple-A starter with elite stuff and stamina, plus movement and an elite splitter and sinker, though a 4.25 ERA over 137 2/3 innings shows he is still refining. David Santiago (No. 91) posted a 2.72 ERA across 145 2/3 innings, and Melvin Canales (No. 33) pairs a plus slider with an elite cutter in relief. Carlos Samaniego (No. 25) hit .316/.390/.495 this season, and Chris Graham (No. 58), the 10th overall pick in the 2032 Draft, brings elite gap power. Eight Top 100 prospects and the seventh-best readiness mark make it a complete package.
25: Montreal makes the largest climb in the rankings, up six spots to No. 9 and tied with Galveston, on an unusual amount of hitting depth: eight of its nine top-200 prospects are bats. Phil Payne (No. 105), a Double-A outfielder with elite power and plus discipline, led the group with 28 home runs and a .281/.401/.539 line, and Bryan Sarro (No. 57) hit 22 with elite gap power and elite speed. Jonathan Anthony (No. 102), now at A-, hit .362/.435/.595 with elite power and discipline, while Elijah Thompson (No. 136), the 21st overall pick in the 2032 Draft, has elite gap power and speed. Chris Shere (No. 24), the lone arm, has plus stuff, control and stamina but a 6.08 ERA at Double-A. With only two Top 100 prospects, the climb rests on depth rather than star power.
26: Huron drops seven spots to No. 25, the third-largest fall in the league, and it is one of only two organizations without a Top 100 prospect, along with Rochester. John Nash (No. 137) is the highest-ranked of the five top-200 names, an outfielder with plus power, discipline and defense despite a below-average hit tool and a .223/.313/.405 line this season. Matt Ray (No. 184), a Double-A designated hitter with plus hit and power, hit .313/.393/.511 with 19 homers, and Rocky Hoyle (No. 173) hit .319/.361/.485 with elite gap power. Joe Hughes (No. 177) has plus movement, elite stamina and a 3.43 ERA with just 1.2 walks per nine, but his stuff grades below average. A well-below-average blue-chip grade defines the problem; any rebound will have to come from depth, which grades average.
27: All five of San Diego's top-200 prospects are at Triple-A, and three of them are pitchers, but the system still slips two spots to No. 22. Jessie Hughes (No. 48), a 21-year-old starter, has plus stuff, movement and control, elite stamina and an elite fastball, though a fragile durability grade and a 4.06 ERA with only 5.7 strikeouts per nine are cautionary. Cesar Castro (No. 95) has elite control and a plus changeup but a fragile grade of his own and a 6.31 ERA, and Aaron Buggage (No. 97) posted a 5.83 ERA despite plus movement. The bats, ranked 31st, are weaker: Willie Perez (No. 153) has a plus hit tool and elite gap power, and catcher Tyler Joyner (No. 183) hit 15 homers. Three Top 100 arms and an elite balance grade cannot fully offset a below-average depth grade.
28: Phoenix slips two spots to No. 27, with the 12th-ranked offense well ahead of the 28th-ranked pitching group. Victor Calderon (No. 100) has plus power, elite gap power and discipline and plus speed and hit .297/.370/.554 this season; Casey Morris (No. 63), a plus defensive shortstop with elite gap power, is also at Triple-A, and Jessie Knotts (No. 96) hit 24 homers. Eric Clements (No. 140), the 27th overall pick in the 2032 Draft, put up .333/.450/.587 at Rookie ball with elite gap power. Willie Villalba (No. 50), a 20-year-old at A with plus stuff, movement and a plus fastball, cutter and sinker, is the one real arm and carried a 2.31 ERA over 93 2/3 innings. Four Top 100 names show upside, but below-average depth and balance and a 23rd readiness rank say it is far from contributing.
213: Rochester sits last at No. 32, the only system besides Huron without a Top 100 prospect, and it has just two names in the top 200. Ian Nelson (No. 175), the 30th overall pick in the 2032 Draft, is the lone hitter, an 18-year-old designated hitter at Rookie ball with elite power and plate discipline who hit .283/.398/.472 with 10 homers this season, though his speed grades below average. Chris King (No. 188) is a 21-year-old starter at A+ with plus movement and elite control, but his stuff is below average and his fragile durability grade is a concern. Batting, pitching and readiness all rank 31st or worse, and blue-chip and depth grades are well below average, so the path back runs through the draft and through Nelson's bat developing on schedule.
214: New York moves up a spot to No. 28, but with one Top 100 prospect and four in the top 200 it remains a thin group. Jessie Marino (No. 72), the seventh overall pick in the 2032 Draft, is the headliner: a Double-A starter with plus movement and a plus changeup and sinker who posted a 3.01 ERA over 68 2/3 innings, even though his control and stamina both grade below average. Joe Weiner (No. 112), a center fielder with plus speed and defense, hit just .229/.272/.351, while Mike Fesperman (No. 191) hit .347/.379/.512 on the strength of a plus hit tool. Greg Tucker (No. 187) has plus control and elite stamina but a 5.72 ERA. A tenth-ranked readiness mark is the one bright spot, since all four of these prospects are at Double-A or Triple-A.
215: One real power bat leads Kansas City's four-spot rise to No. 20. Pedro Huante (No. 31), a 22-year-old outfielder at Double-A with plus power, hit .282/.370/.478 this season and led the group with 24 home runs. Josh Herrington (No. 87) is the only arm, a Double-A starter with plus movement and control but below-average stuff, who posted a 3.38 ERA with 2.2 walks per nine over 136 innings. Tim Gouldman (No. 120) has a plus hit tool and plus speed at A+, though his power grades below average. Three top-200 prospects and a below-average blue-chip grade make this a thin system, and average depth and balance grades say the pipeline needs reinforcements from the draft to climb further.
216: One name defines Mexico City, which holds at No. 30. Kevin Clarke (No. 11), a 22-year-old outfielder at Double-A, has plus hit, power and gap power and below-average speed, and he hit .265/.356/.408 with 15 homers this season; he is the only Top 100 prospect the organization has. Adam Brady (No. 110) is a 25-year-old at Triple-A with plus gap power who hit .313/.375/.526, and Bobby Kraemer (No. 103) is a durable catcher at Double-A. All three top-200 prospects are hitters, the pitching rank is 29th and the depth grade is well below average, so any improvement will have to come from adding arms and numbers beneath Clarke.
